title: A Distant Star is Slowly Snacking on a Brown Dwarf - Nautilus
gist: Astronomers have for the first time directly observed a red dwarf star slowly accreting material from a nearby brown dwarf, an intermediate state between stable orbit and rapid consumption that could take billions of years to finish.

insights.claim: Star-planet relationships are usually framed as one of two outcomes: a stable fixed orbit, or a body that flies too close and is consumed by its star.
insights.speaker: David Nield
insights.so_what: Sets up the binary model that the new observation complicates.
insights.quote: Either a planet orbits its star in a fixed and stable circuit, or it flies too close to the sun (literally) and gets consumed by stellar wind and fire.
insights.locator: Planets and stars usually have one

insights.claim: Astronomers have for the first time directly observed an in-between state in which a red dwarf star is absorbing material from a nearby brown dwarf very slowly.
insights.speaker: David Nield
insights.so_what: A first-of-kind observation expanding models of how stellar companions evolve.
insights.quote: for the first time, astronomers have directly observed an in-between state, a red dwarf star that’s absorbing material from a nearby brown dwarf, but very, very slowly
insights.locator: But now, for the first time

insights.claim: The accretion of brown dwarf material onto the red dwarf is so slow that it may take billions of years before the brown dwarf disappears entirely.
insights.speaker: David Nield
insights.so_what: Implies such slow-accretion systems could be long-lived and potentially more common than previously detected.
insights.quote: it might be billions of years before the brown dwarf disappears altogether
insights.locator: But now, for the first time
